title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the 35th Batch of Guiding Cases
ruling_gist_en: Facial information processed by facial recognition technology and facial information generated on the basis of facial recognition technology are both highly identifiable and can, individually or in combination with other information, identify a specific natural person's identity or reflect the activities of a specific natural person, and therefore constitute citizens' personal information as defined by the Criminal Law. Where a person, without the consent of the citizen concerned and without any lawful ground for processing personal information under the Personal Information Protection Law (such as legal authorization or authorization from relevant departments), steals or otherwise illegally obtains the aforementioned information by using software programs or other methods, if the circumstances are serious, the person shall be convicted and punished in accordance with Article 5, paragraph 1, item 4 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court and the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Handling of Criminal Cases of Infringement upon Citizens' Personal Information, and other relevant provisions.
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice on Issuing the 35th Batch of Guiding Cases

Fa [2022] No. 265

To the High People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government; the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army; and the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the High People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

Upon deliberation and decision by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, the following four cases (Guiding Cases No. 192-195), including Li Kaixiang's criminal附带 civil public interest litigation for infringement of citizens' personal information, are hereby issued as the 35th batch of guiding cases for reference in adjudicating similar cases.

December 26, 2022

Guiding Case No. 192

Li Kaixiang v. [Procuratorial Authority] — criminal附带 civil public interest litigation for infringement of citizens' personal information

(Deliberated and approved by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, issued on December 26, 2022)

Keywords: criminal; infringement of citizens' personal information; criminal附带 civil public interest litigation; facial recognition; facial information

Ruling Gist

Facial information processed using facial recognition technology and facial information generated based on facial recognition technology both have a high degree of identifiability. They can, alone or in combination with other information, identify the identity of a specific natural person or reflect the activities of a specific natural person, and thus constitute "citizens' personal information" as defined in the Criminal Law. Where a perpetrator, without the consent of the citizen himself or herself and without lawful grounds for processing personal information as prescribed by the Personal Information Protection Law (such as legal authorization or authorization by relevant departments), steals or otherwise illegally obtains the above information through software programs or other means, and the circumstances are serious, the perpetrator shall be convicted and punished in accordance with Article 5, Paragraph 1, Item 4 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court and the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Criminal Cases Involving Infringement of Citizens' Personal Information, among other provisions.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 253a of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

Between June and September 2020, the defendant Li Kaixiang created a mobile phone "hacker software" with the function of illegally stealing photos from the album of the installer, packaged it into an "APK installation package" for the Android mobile terminal, published it for sale on the "Chama Ancient Road" forum on the dark web, and disguised it as a "beauty detection" software and published it on the "Jiezi Forum" (later renamed "Kuaimao Community") for free download by visitors. When users downloaded and installed the "beauty detection" software for use, the software would automatically retrieve photos from the mobile phone album in the background and automatically upload them to the Tencent Cloud server backend set up by the defendant, thereby stealing a total of 1,751 photos from the installers' albums, some of which contained over 100 pieces of citizens' personal information such as facial information, natural persons' names, identification numbers, contact information, and home addresses.

In September 2020, the defendant Li Kaixiang saw a "hacker data" post on the "Chama Ancient Road" forum on the dark web. He then used part of the proceeds from his previous sale of the "APK installation package" on the dark web to purchase and download data titled "Social Engineering Database Data" and transferred it to the "MEGA" cloud drive. After his own review, he confirmed that it contained real personal information. In February 2021, although the defendant Li Kaixiang knew that the "Social Engineering Database Data" contained household registration information, QQ account registration information, JD account registration information, vehicle owner information, loan information, etc., he still shared the cloud drive link to the "Cuihu Manor Owners' Exchange" QQ group, of which he was an administrator, for free download by group members. According to expert evaluation, after removing invalid data and merging and deduplicating, the "Social Engineering Database Data" contained a total of over 81 million pieces of various types of citizens' personal information.

The People's Procuratorate of Fengxian District, Shanghai, initiated a criminal附带 civil public interest lawsuit on the grounds that social public interests were harmed.

The defendant Li Kaixiang had no objection to the basic criminal facts and the nature of the crime charged, and voluntarily confessed and accepted punishment.

Defense counsel argued that the defendant Li Kaixiang was a first-time offender, truthfully confessed his crimes after arrival at the case, and voluntarily confessed and accepted punishment, and requested a lighter punishment and a suspended sentence for the defendant Li Kaixiang. Defense counsel further argued that the procuratorial authority had not verified and confirmed the authenticity of the over 81 million pieces of data information involved.

Judgment

On August 23, 2021, the People's Court of Fengxian District, Shanghai, rendered criminal judgment (2021) Hu 0120 Xing Chu No. 828, finding the defendant Li Kaixiang guilty of the crime of infringing citizens' personal information, sentencing him to three years' imprisonment with a three-year suspension, and imposing a fine of RMB 10,000; the criminal tools seized were confiscated. The judgment ordered Li Kaixiang to publicly apologize on a national news media outlet for his act of infringing citizens' personal information, delete the "beauty detection" software and related codes, delete the photos involved stored on Tencent Cloud drive, delete the relevant citizens' personal information stored on the "MEGA" cloud drive, and cancel the QQ number used for the infringement. After the first-instance judgment, there was no protest or appeal, and the judgment has now taken effect.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: The focus of dispute in this case is whether the "facial information" stolen using the "beauty detection" software involved falls within the category of "citizens' personal information" regulated by criminal law. After trial, the court held that "facial information" constitutes citizens' personal information as defined in Article 253a of the Criminal Law, and the act of using the "beauty detection" hacker software to steal "facial information" and other citizens' personal information of software users constitutes the act of "stealing or otherwise illegally obtaining citizens' personal information" under the Criminal Law, and should be punished according to law. The main reasons are as follows: First, "facial information" and other explicitly enumerated types of personal information both have obvious "identifiability" characteristics. The Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court and the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Criminal Cases Involving Infringement of Citizens' Personal Information (hereinafter referred to as the "Interpretation") enumerates the types of citizens' personal information. Although it does not separately enumerate "facial information," it allows for the recognition of other forms of personal information beyond the enumeration according to law. The definition and explicit enumeration of citizens' personal information in the Interpretation are consistent with the criteria for identifying citizens' personal information in laws such as the Civil Code, which takes "identifiability" as the standard for identifying personal information, emphasizing the possibility of directly or indirectly identifying the relationship between the information and the data subject. "Facial information" belongs to biometric information, which has immutability and uniqueness. A face corresponds one-to-one with a specific natural person and can directly identify a specific natural person without the need to combine with other information, thus having extremely high "identifiability." Second, the recognition of "facial information" as citizens' personal information follows the principle of unity of legal order. Preceding laws such as the civil law protect "facial information" as citizens' personal information. Article 1034 of the Civil Code defines the concept and specific types of personal information. The Personal Information Protection Law further includes "facial information" within the scope of protection of personal information. Where the act of infringing on "facial information" constitutes infringement of natural persons' personality rights and other rights, the perpetrator shall bear corresponding civil liability or administrative and criminal liability. Third, using the "beauty detection" hacker software to steal "facial information" has significant social harm and criminal punishability. Because "facial information" is a sensitive information for identifying a specific individual, and it is also personal information with strong social attributes and easy to collect, it is highly likely to be directly used or synthesized by others to bypass facial recognition verification procedures, leading to illegal acts such as infringing on privacy rights, reputation rights, and even criminal acts such as theft and fraud, causing great social harm. The defendant Li Kaixiang manipulated the "beauty detection" software disguised as hacker software to steal users' selfies and photos stored in their mobile phone albums, exploiting the openness of the internet platform, targeting unspecified members of the public, with covert means, strong deception, and wide scope of theft, which has obvious social harm and requires regulation by criminal law.

Regarding the defense opinion that the basis for determining the quantity of citizens' personal information in this case was insufficient, the court found through trial that during the investigation process, the public security authority adopted a sampling verification method, randomly selecting part of the personal information for verification, and was able to confirm the authenticity of the personal information involved. The defendant and defense counsel did not provide any leads or evidence that the involved information was not authentic. The judicial appraisal institution removed invalid information and used a method of merging and deduplicating to appraise, detecting 81 million pieces of valid personal information. The quantity of citizens' personal information charged by the prosecutorial authority was objective and authentic, and was in line with the rules for determining the specific quantity of批量 citizens' personal information established in the Interpretation. Therefore, the defense opinion was not adopted.

In summary, the defendant Li Kaixiang, in violation of relevant state regulations, illegally obtained and provided citizens' personal information to others, with particularly serious circumstances, and his conduct constituted the crime of infringing citizens' personal information. After arriving at the case, the defendant Li Kaixiang could truthfully confess his crimes and could be given a lighter punishment according to law, and he voluntarily confessed and accepted punishment, so he could be given a lenient punishment according to law. The tortious act of Li Kaixiang illegally obtaining and providing citizens' personal information to others infringed on the personal information security of numerous citizens, harmed social public interests, and he should bear corresponding civil liability. Accordingly, the above judgment was rendered according to law.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Li Xiaojie, Guan Yujie, Gao Yetao)

Guiding Case No. 193

Wen Wei et al. v. [Procuratorial Authority] — infringement of citizens' personal information

(Deliberated and approved by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, issued on December 26, 2022)

Keywords: criminal; infringement of citizens' personal information; resident identity card information

Ruling Gist

Resident identity card information includes multiple types of personal information such as the natural person's name, facial recognition information, identity number, and household registration address. It falls within the category of "other citizens' personal information that may affect personal or property safety" as provided in Article 5, Paragraph 1, Item 4 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court and the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Criminal Cases Involving Infringement of Citizens' Personal Information. The illegal acquisition, sale, or provision of resident identity card information, where the circumstances are serious, constitutes the crime of infringing citizens' personal information under Article 253a(1) of the Criminal Law.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 253a of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

Between June and August 2019, the defendant Wen Wei (then the operation director of Shanghai Haoti Information Technology Co., Ltd.), after prior contact, agreed with persons with WeChat and QQ usernames "Fale," "Laizhongzhong," and "I am afraid of the cold wind" etc. to batch register and activate the "BOC Pass · Magic Yuan" co-branded prepaid cards for the company's "Love Ball Wallet" APP application at a price of RMB 6 per card. From the above persons, he obtained citizens' personal information (front and back photos of resident identity cards) through WeChat and QQ by obtaining Baidu Netdisk sharing links. The defendant Zhu Xudong downloaded the information from the netdisk link to a mobile hard drive and handed it over to BOC Pass staff for batch registration and activation.

Between September 2019 and February 2020, after defendant Wen Wei left his position, defendant Zhu Xudong was responsible for the batch registration and activation of the above co-branded prepaid cards. By the same method as above, at a price of RMB 6 per card, he continued to obtain citizens' personal information (front and back photos of resident identity cards) from "Fale," "Laizhongzhong," "I am afraid of the cold wind," etc., through WeChat and QQ by obtaining Baidu Netdisk sharing links, stored them in his Baidu Netdisk, then downloaded them to his computer hard drive, and handed them over to BOC Pass staff for batch registration and activation.

In October 2019, after prior contact via WeChat, defendant Zhu Xudong and Zhang Kun (separately prosecuted) agreed that at a price of RMB 6 per card, by the same method as above, Zhu Xudong obtained citizens' personal information (front and back photos of resident identity cards) from Zhang Kun through QQ by obtaining Baidu Netdisk sharing links, stored them in his Baidu Netdisk, then downloaded them to his computer hard drive, and handed them over to BOC Pass staff for batch registration and activation.

In December 2019, defendant Zhang Jiangtao purchased citizens' personal information data from others through his QQ group and transferred it to his Baidu Netdisk account, and also sold the data to Zhang Kun in multiple installments, receiving a total of RMB 19,600 yuan in multiple payments.

Upon verification, from the netdisk of defendant Wen Wei "ErnieGullit," over 10,000 sets of citizens' personal information (front and back photos of resident identity cards) were inventoried; from the netdisk of defendant Zhu Xudong "zhuxudn," over 3,000 sets of citizens' personal information (front and back photos of resident identity cards) were inventoried; from the netdisk shared by Zhang Kun to Zhu Xudong, 41,654 sets of citizens' personal information (front and back photos of resident identity cards) were inventoried; from the netdisk of defendant Zhang Jiangtao, 60,101 sets of citizens' personal information were inventoried.

The People's Procuratorate of Hongkou District, Shanghai, charged the defendants Wen Wei, Zhu Xudong, and Zhang Jiangtao with the crime of infringing citizens' personal information, with particularly serious circumstances, and their conduct should all be investigated for criminal liability for the crime of infringing citizens' personal information.

The defense counsels for both defendants Wen Wei and Zhu Xudong argued that the type of citizen information charged in this case should be recognized as the ordinary information scope under Article 5, Paragraph 1, Item 5 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court and the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Criminal Cases Involving Infringement of Citizens' Personal Information (hereinafter referred to as the "Interpretation"), not the specific information type scope under Item 4 of Paragraph 1 of the same Article. Therefore, based on the currently discovered quantity, the circumstances had not yet constituted "particularly serious."

Judgment

On August 30, 2021, the People's Court of Hongkou District, Shanghai, rendered criminal judgment (2020) Hu 0109 Xing Chu No. 957, finding defendant Wen Wei guilty of the crime of infringing citizens' personal information, sentencing him to three years' imprisonment, and imposing a fine of RMB 10,000; defendant Zhu Xudong guilty of the crime of infringing citizens' personal information, sentencing him to three years and three months' imprisonment, and imposing a fine of RMB 10,000; defendant Zhang Jiangtao guilty of the crime of infringing citizens' personal information, sentencing him to three years' imprisonment, and imposing a fine of RMB 20,000; illegal gains and criminal tools were ordered to be recovered and confiscated. After the verdict, defendants Wen Wei and Zhu Xudong appealed. On November 11, 2021, the Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court rendered criminal ruling (2021) Hu 02 Xing Zhong No. 1055, rejecting the appeal and affirming the original judgment.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: The focus of dispute in this case is whether the resident identity card information involved falls within "other citizens' personal information that may affect personal or property safety" under Article 5, Paragraph 1, Item 4 of the Interpretation. According to Article 5, Paragraph 1, Item 4 of the Interpretation, illegally obtaining, selling, or providing 500 or more pieces of citizens' personal information such as accommodation information, communication information, health and physiological information, transaction information, or other citizens' personal information that may affect personal or property safety may be deemed as "serious circumstances." Item 5 of the same paragraph provides that illegally obtaining, selling, or providing 5,000 or more pieces of citizens' personal information other than those specified in Items 3 and 4 of the same paragraph may be deemed as "serious circumstances." That is, if the resident identity card information involved is recognized as "other citizens' personal information that may affect personal or property safety" under Item 4 of Paragraph 1 of Article 5 of the Interpretation, then the transaction of 500 or more pieces of such personal information may be deemed as "serious circumstances," and 5,000 or more pieces constitute "particularly serious circumstances."

The first-instance court found through trial that the address on a resident identity card is either the citizen's actual residential address or nominal household registration address. Either way, it has a very close and important connection with the personal and property safety of the citizen and his or her family. The illegal disclosure or leak of a home address will pose a major risk to the personal and property safety of the citizen and his or her family, opening the door for precise implementation of various illegal and criminal activities. Therefore, it should be given priority protection. From the general legal interpretation principle of "arguing from the lighter to the heavier," its importance should also be higher than "accommodation information," which is a temporary or past residence of a citizen. Hence, it should be recognized as the type of information specified in Item 4 of Paragraph 1 of Article 5 of the Interpretation.

The second-instance court found through trial that a resident identity card not only contains household registration address information, but also is a composite of the citizen's name, facial information, unique identity number, and other information. It is an important identification document for citizens. In the information network society, the entirety of resident identity card information is sensitive information, which can be used to register, authenticate, and bind network accounts. The citizens' personal information formed by combining the citizen's facial information, identity number, name, and address information has uniqueness, can be precisely matched with the individual citizen, and can induce further leakage of other personal information of the citizen, causing great harm to the citizen's personal information rights and interests. The entire resident identity card information should be recognized as information concerning the citizen's personal and property safety. Although the first-instance and second-instance courts had different reasoning and standards, their conclusions were consistent. The court held that the first-instance court's conviction and application of law for Wen Wei and Zhu Xudong were correct, the sentences based on their criminal means and circumstances were not improper, and the trial procedure was lawful. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed and the original judgment was affirmed.

(Judges of the effective judgment: Zhang Song, Bai Nan, Zhang Pengfei)

Guiding Case No. 194

Xiong Changheng et al. v. [Procuratorial Authority] — infringement of citizens' personal information

(Deliberated and approved by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, issued on December 26, 2022)

Keywords: criminal; infringement of citizens' personal information; WeChat account; social media account; illegal acquisition; reasonable processing

Ruling Gist

1. In violation of relevant state regulations, purchasing social media accounts such as WeChat accounts that have been registered but not yet used, and through marketing software with functions such as intelligent group sending, adding friends, and establishing discussion groups, illegally producing and selling or providing to others social media accounts such as WeChat accounts that carry citizens' personal information and can be used for social activities, where the circumstances are serious, constitutes the act of "in violation of relevant state regulations, selling or providing citizens' personal information to others" under Article 253a(1) of the Criminal Law, and constitutes the crime of infringing citizens' personal information.

2. Without the consent of the citizen himself or herself, or without having a reason prescribed by the Personal Information Protection Law such as legal authorization, acquiring citizens' personal information that has been disclosed within a certain scope through means such as purchase, receipt, or exchange for illegal use, thereby changing the scope, purpose, and nature of the disclosure of the citizen's personal information, does not constitute reasonable processing as defined by law, and constitutes the act of "illegally obtaining citizens' personal information by other means" under Article 253a(3) of the Criminal Law. Where the circumstances are serious, it constitutes the crime of infringing citizens' personal information.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 253a of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

In June 2020, the defendant Xiong Changheng gathered the defendants Xiong Changlin, Xiong Gonglang, and Xiong Changqiang to engage in the business of selling ready-made WeChat accounts loaded with citizens' personal information that could be used for social activities. Due to lack of experience, profits were low during this period. To seek greater profits, at the end of September 2020, the defendants Xiong Changheng, Xiong Changlin, Xiong Gonglang, and Xiong Changqiang jointly invested to purchase online a software called "Wei Qibing" (a marketing software based on the computer version of WeChat, featuring multi-opening, multi-account intelligent mass messaging, adding people, group building, group removal, and follower cleanup), which was used to illegally add WeChat friends and create ready-made WeChat accounts for sale. In October 2020, the defendant Xiong Changheng's friend Qin Yingbin (at large) invested RMB 50,000 (holding 40% shares), Xiong Changheng invested RMB 20,000 (holding 20% shares), the defendants Xiong Changlin, Xiong Gonglang, and Xiong Changqiang each contributed a certain number of computers and mobile phones (each holding 10% shares), and the defendant Fan Jiacong did not invest (holding 5% shares); the remaining 5% of share profits were used for the company's daily expenses. Subsequently, they jointly purchased office desks, computers, second-hand mobile phones, and other items, rented a location at Linglong Pavilion, Wuhua Road, Hezhou Street, Fengcheng City, Jiangxi Province, and established the "Fengcheng Changwen Trading Company" under a signboard. Qin Yingbin was responsible for externally purchasing blank WeChat accounts and selling finished WeChat accounts. The defendant Xiong Changheng was responsible for internal company management and hiring company employees. The defendants Xiong Changlin, Xiong Gonglang, Xiong Changqiang, and Fan Jiacong, together with the hired company employees, directly participated in illegally creating finished WeChat accounts using the "Wei Qibing" software. The finished WeChat accounts were then sold at high prices through Qin Yingbin, thereby illegally obtaining profits.

In January 2021, the defendants Xiong Changheng, Xiong Changlin, Xiong Gonglang, Xiong Changqiang, and Fan Jiacong, together with Qin Yingbin, while selling finished WeChat accounts, also illegally obtained job seekers' personal information (including name, gender, phone number, and other basic personal identity information of citizens) through online purchases, and then distributed the job seekers' information to company staff. Using a reward method where employees earned approximately RMB 10 in commission for each job seeker's WeChat account they added, the employees falsely claimed to be staff of "Gongke Technology Media" and, using prepared scripts, asked job seekers to add a "mentor's" WeChat on the pretext of part-time tasks such as fake orders, thereby luring victims into groups and causing some victims to be defrauded.

During the operation period, after paying wages and related expenses, the defendants Xiong Changheng, Xiong Changlin, Xiong Gonglang, Xiong Changqiang, and Fan Jiacong, together with Qin Yingbin, obtained total dividends of over RMB 200,000, which were distributed according to their respective shareholdings. The specific profits obtained were as follows: defendant Xiong Changheng over RMB 58,000, defendant Xiong Changlin over RMB 29,000, defendant Xiong Gonglang over RMB 29,000, defendant Xiong Changqiang over RMB 29,000, and defendant Fan Jiacong over RMB 14,500.

Judgment

The Fengcheng City People's Court of Jiangxi Province, by criminal judgment (2021) Gan 0981 Xingchu No. 376 dated September 23, 2021, found the defendant Xiong Changheng guilty of the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information, sentencing him to three years and two months of fixed-term imprisonment and a fine of RMB 100,000; the defendant Xiong Changlin guilty of the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information, sentencing him to one year and ten months of fixed-term imprisonment and a fine of RMB 60,000; the defendant Xiong Gonglang guilty of the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information, sentencing him to one year and ten months of fixed-term imprisonment and a fine of RMB 60,000; the defendant Xiong Changqiang guilty of the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information, sentencing him to one year and ten months of fixed-term imprisonment and a fine of RMB 60,000; the defendant Fan Jiacong guilty of the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information, sentencing him to ten months of fixed-term imprisonment and a fine of RMB 30,000 (already paid); the illegal gains of RMB 14,500 voluntarily surrendered by the defendant Fan Jiacong were confiscated and turned over to the state treasury; the continued recovery of the illegal gains of defendant Xiong Changheng of RMB 58,000, defendant Xiong Changlin of RMB 29,000, defendant Xiong Gonglang of RMB 29,000, and defendant Xiong Changqiang of RMB 29,000 was ordered, to be confiscated and turned over to the state treasury; the confiscated mobile phones were ordered to be confiscated and handled by the confiscating authority according to law.

Reasoning

The effective judgment held that the defendants Xiong Changheng and others, in violation of relevant state regulations, jointly invested in purchasing blank WeChat accounts and a marketing software for intelligent mass messaging, adding people, and group building, as well as purchasing others' job seekers' information through the internet, illegally adding WeChat friends, creating finished WeChat accounts for sale, or providing illegally obtained citizens' personal information to others, and profited therefrom. The circumstances were particularly serious, and their actions constituted the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information. Citizens' personal information in this crime refers to information that is closely related to an individual citizen and that the individual does not wish to be known by persons other than a specific group. If the illegally obtained citizens' personal information belongs to citizens' privacy information or information that may cause extremely adverse consequences after disclosure, it not only seriously infringes upon citizens' personal information security and lawful rights and interests but also provides assistance for illegal and criminal activities such as online gambling and telecommunications network fraud, seriously disrupting public order and posing great social harm. WeChat not only serves as a communication tool but also has functions such as social networking and payment. WeChat accounts are bound to mobile phone real-name registrations, bound to bank cards, and correspond one-to-one with natural persons, so WeChat accounts can be considered citizens' personal information.

The defendants illegally processed publicly available personal information and profited therefrom, violating the purpose of the disclosure of such information or significantly changing its use. After the information was further utilized, it endangered the personal or property safety of individuals. The circumstances were particularly serious, and their actions constituted the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information.

In summary, without obtaining the consent and authorization of the rights holders, each defendant illegally obtained others' WeChat accounts and resold them for profit, or illegally processed publicly available citizens' personal information, exposing others' personal information to the risk of leakage and loss of control, and obtained huge illegal gains therefrom. Their actions violated state regulations, infringed upon citizens' personal information rights, and constituted the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information.

(Trial judges of the effective judgment: Wang Yuehua, Hu Yibo, Li Luanfang)

Guiding Case No. 195

Luo Wenjun and Qu Xiaozhen — criminal附带 civil public interest litigation for infringing upon citizens' personal information

(Discussed and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on December 26, 2022)

Keywords Criminal / Infringement upon citizens' personal information / Verification codes / Sale

Ruling Gist

Verification codes, composed of individual or combined numbers, letters, etc., specifically sent by service providers to particular mobile phone numbers, are unique and confidential. If they can individually or in combination with other information identify the identity of a specific natural person or reflect the activities of a specific natural person, they fall within the definition of citizens' personal information under the Criminal Law. Where a perpetrator sells to others verification codes and corresponding mobile phone numbers obtained in the course of providing services, and the circumstances are serious, the perpetrator shall be convicted and punished according to the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Article 253-1 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

In December 2019, the defendant Luo Wenjun learned that money could be made by obtaining others' mobile phone numbers and random verification codes to register new accounts on apps such as Taobao and JD.com (referred to as "La Xin" or pulling new users). He then contacted persons specializing in "La Xin" with WeChat nicknames such as "Youyou 141319" (identity unknown), "A Wo Yi Cheng Nian Ai Shui Shui" (identity unknown), "Jie Jing Tao" (identity unknown), "Pang E" (identity unknown), and "Hei Bei Hei Zhiwei 80 Hou De Jian Zheng" (identity unknown). After "Youyou 141319" and others learned that Luo Wenjun had many trainees who were telecommunications employees and could directly obtain customers' mobile phone numbers and random verification codes, they took advantage of Luo Wenjun's position as a training instructor at a telecommunications company. They agreed that Luo Wenjun would establish, manage, and maintain WeChat groups and announce the rules, requirements, and specific prices for "La Xin" within the groups; the trainees, according to the requirements, would send the illegally obtained customer mobile phone numbers and random verification codes into the groups; "Youyou 141319" and others would use the sent mobile phone numbers and verification codes to register new accounts on Taobao, JD.com, etc. Luo Wenjun could receive compensation of RMB 0.2 to 2 yuan per successfully "La Xin" mobile phone number information; the trainees received compensation ranging from RMB 1 to 13 yuan per item, distributed by Luo Wenjun or directly sent by "Youyou 141319" and others to the trainees according to the announced prices in the groups.

From December 2019 to July 2021, the defendant Luo Wenjun, taking advantage of the positions of Qu Xiaozhen, a salesperson at Zhuzhou Liansheng Communication Co., Ltd. Lukou Mobile Phone Store and China Mobile Business Hall, as well as Xie Qing, Huang Ying, and He Changqing (all three have been subjected to administrative penalties), illegally obtained and sold the personal information, including mobile phone numbers and random verification codes, of victims Peng Moumou and Tan Moumou to "Youyou 141319" and others. Among them, defendant Luo Wenjun profited RMB 13,000, and defendant Qu Xiaozhen profited RMB 9,266.5.

After the incident, defendant Qu Xiaozhen had already surrendered illegal gains of RMB 9,926.5 (as determined by the investigatory authority), and Luo Wenjun had surrendered illegal gains of RMB 13,000. Both defendants Luo Wenjun and Qu Xiaozhen truthfully confessed their criminal facts and voluntarily admitted guilt and accepted punishment.

It was also found that the Zhuzhou City Lukou District People's Procuratorate announced the case on July 22, 2021. During the announcement period, no legally prescribed authorities or relevant organizations filed civil public interest litigation, meaning the Zhuzhou City Lukou District People's Procuratorate was the proper subject to initiate the accompanying civil public interest litigation.

Judgment

The Lukou District People's Court of Zhuzhou City, Hunan Province, by criminal judgment (2021) Xiang 0212 Xingchu No. 149 dated November 30, 2021, found the defendant Luo Wenjun guilty of the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information, sentencing him to eight months of fixed-term imprisonment and a fine of RMB 20,000. The defendant Qu Xiaozhen was found guilty of the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information, sentencing her to six months of fixed-term imprisonment and a fine of RMB 15,000. The tools of crime, one OPPO RENO mobile phone and one Huawei P30 Pro mobile phone, were confiscated and handled according to law. The illegal gains of defendant Luo Wenjun of RMB 13,000 and defendant Qu Xiaozhen of RMB 9,266.5 were confiscated and turned over to the state treasury.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that the defendant Luo Wenjun, in violation of relevant state regulations, established a communication group for selling and providing citizens' personal information, with serious circumstances. His actions simultaneously constituted the crime of illegally using information networks and the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information; according to law, he should be convicted of the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information. The defendant Qu Xiaozhen, in violation of relevant state regulations, sold citizens' personal information obtained in the course of providing services to others, with serious circumstances. Her actions constituted the crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information. The facts and charges of the crime as alleged by the public prosecutor were established, and the court supported them.

In the joint crime, the defendants Luo Wenjun and Qu Xiaozhen played equivalent roles and should both be considered principal offenders. The defendant Qu Xiaozhen sold citizens' personal information obtained in the course of providing services to others, which should be subject to heavier punishment. Luo Wenjun and Qu Xiaozhen, after being brought to justice, truthfully confessed all criminal facts, both showing frankness, actively surrendered all illicit gains, and admitted guilt and accepted punishment, thus could be dealt with leniently. The sentencing recommendations from the public prosecutor were appropriate and were adopted.

Luo Wenjun's defense counsel argued that mobile phone numbers and verification codes do not constitute personal information, and that the "La Xin" activity did not cause specific losses. Upon investigation, personal information refers to various information recorded electronically or by other means that can identify a specific natural person individually or in combination with other information, including telephone numbers, etc. Verification codes are unique numerical combinations specifically sent to particular mobile phone numbers and, according to regulations, cannot be sent to others, proving that verification codes constitute communication content identifying and verifying personal identity; that is, both are personal information that can identify a natural person's identity. The crime of infringing upon citizens' personal information does not require causing specific losses as a constitutive element; therefore, this defense argument was not adopted.

Luo Wenjun's defense counsel argued that Luo Wenjun did not personally provide mobile phone numbers and verification codes. Upon investigation, Luo Wenjun not only gathered Qu Xiaozhen and others for "La Xin" but also specifically established communication groups for providing and selling citizens' personal information for illegal and criminal activities, thereby profiting, and should be subject to heavier punishment according to law; thus, this argument was not adopted.

Luo Wenjun's defense counsel argued for a suspended sentence for Luo Wenjun. Upon investigation, considering the circumstances of the crime, the degree of social harm, and the defendant's expression of remorse, a suspended sentence was not applicable to defendant Luo Wenjun; thus, this argument was not adopted. However, the defense counsel's other arguments regarding possible lighter punishment for Luo Wenjun were consistent with the facts and were adopted.

Qu Xiaozhen's defense counsel argued that Qu Xiaozhen had meritorious service. Upon investigation, Qu Xiaozhen provided basic information such as Luo Wenjun's address and contact information, which were facts she should have disclosed and were related to her own criminal conduct, and did not constitute meritorious service; thus, this argument was not adopted. The defense counsel's other arguments regarding possible lighter punishment were consistent with the facts and were adopted.

The defendants Luo Wenjun and Qu Xiaozhen infringed upon citizens' personal information. While bearing criminal liability, they should also bear corresponding civil liability. Given that both defendants had no objection to the infringement and both expressed willingness to publicly apologize and permanently delete the involved personal information, the claims of the plaintiff in the accompanying civil public interest litigation were supported.

(Trial judges of the effective judgment: Wang Xin, Zhou Xiaoling, Lai Guoqing, Liu Zhiqun, Liu Yun, Yuan Shuilian, Cao Yuting)
